LONDON, England (CNN) -- More than 150 people have abandoned a sinking cruise liner that collided with an iceberg in Antarctic waters, a Chilean navy captain told CNN. The ship sent out a distress call at around 10 p.m. ET Thursday. Passenger ship Explorer reported problems near the South Shetland Islands, south of Argentina. The area is in a sector of Antarctica claimed by the United Kingdom. Capt. Carlos Munita of the Chilean navy said they received a distress call from the Explorer, saying the vessel had hit an iceberg around 10 p.m. ET Thursday. He added a Norwegian rescue ship had arrived at the scene. Tour companies describe the Explorer as a passenger ship which runs tours between South America and Antarctica. Some 154 people are reported to be on board ship, which carries a Liberian flag, including 100 passengers. However the nationalities of those on board is not yet known. Passengers and crew have been evacuated onto lifeboats, but the captain and the first officer are reported to have stayed on board. "The great majority of people, including all the passengers, have been safely taken off the Explorer and are now being recovered by the first of the vessels to arrive on scene in response to the distress call," Dave Jardine-Smith, head of the Maritime and Coastguard Agency's (MCA) search and rescue team in England said. "The passengers and crew from the Explorer have not been in lifeboats very long," Jardine-Smith said. "They should be, hopefully, in good condition. We are told that there are no injuries." Earlier, Mark Clark, a spokesman for the MCA told the Press Association five ships were on their way to help the sinking vessel. "She hit something and is taking on a serious amount of water, that is all we know." The temperature in the area is said to be at around minus 5C, with a sea temperature at around minus 1C, forecasters told the Press Association. Stephen Davenport, senior forecaster with MeteoGroup, said:"It wouldn't take long for hypothermia to set in at that kind of temperature in the sea. "They do get very bad storms down that way, and gale force winds especially, because there is no land in the way," he told PA. Lt. **LONDON, England (CNN) --** More than 150 people have abandoned a sinking cruise liner after it collided with an iceberg in Antarctic waters, a Chilean navy captain told CNN.

The passenger ship *Explorer* sent out a distress call at around 10 p.m. ET Thursday after reporting problems near the South Shetland Islands, south of Argentina. The area lies within a sector of Antarctica claimed by the United Kingdom.

Capt. Carlos Munita of the Chilean navy said authorities received a distress call from the *Explorer* stating that the vessel had struck an iceberg at around 10 p.m. ET Thursday. He added that a Norwegian rescue ship had arrived at the scene.

Tour companies describe the *Explorer* as a passenger ship that operates tours between South America and Antarctica. Approximately 154 people are reported to have been on board the Liberian-flagged vessel, including 100 passengers. However, the nationalities of those on board are not yet known.

Passengers and crew members were evacuated to lifeboats, although the captain and first officer reportedly remained on board.

“The great majority of people, including all the passengers, have been safely taken off the *Explorer* and are now being recovered by the first of the vessels to arrive on scene in response to the distress call,” said Dave Jardine-Smith, head of the Maritime and Coastguard Agency’s (MCA) search and rescue team in England.

“The passengers and crew from the *Explorer* have not been in lifeboats very long,” Jardine-Smith said. “They should be, hopefully, in good condition. We are told that there are no injuries.”

Earlier, MCA spokesman Mark Clark told the Press Association that five ships were on their way to assist the sinking vessel.

“She hit something and is taking on a serious amount of water; that is all we know.”

Forecasters told the Press Association that the air temperature in the area was around minus 5°C, while the sea temperature was approximately minus 1°C.

“It wouldn’t take long for hypothermia to set in at that kind of temperature in the sea,” said Stephen Davenport, a senior forecaster with MeteoGroup.

“They do get very bad storms down that way, and gale-force winds especially, because there is no land in the way,” he told PA.

Lt. Matt Alex of the U.S. Coast Guard Atlantic Area command center said the vessel is owned by Gap Adventures, based in Toronto, Canada.

outputs.L2:
LONDON, England (CNN) — A cruise vessel carrying more than 150 people was sinking after striking an iceberg near Antarctica, according to a Chilean naval captain.

The Liberian-flagged Explorer reported the collision and issued an emergency signal at approximately 10 p.m. ET on Thursday, Capt. Carlos Munita of the Chilean navy told CNN. The incident occurred near the South Shetland Islands, south of Argentina, in an Antarctic region claimed by the United Kingdom.

Munita said a Norwegian rescue vessel had reached the location. Five ships had earlier been heading toward the Explorer to provide assistance, Maritime and Coastguard Agency spokesman Mark Clark told the Press Association.

Tour operators identify the Explorer as a passenger vessel offering trips between South America and Antarctica. Reports indicated that 154 people were aboard, including 100 passengers, although their nationalities were not immediately known.

The passengers and crew evacuated into lifeboats, while the captain and first officer reportedly remained on the ship.

Dave Jardine-Smith, who leads the English Maritime and Coastguard Agency’s search-and-rescue team, said nearly everyone aboard—including every passenger—had been safely removed from the Explorer. The first responding vessel was in the process of picking them up.

Jardine-Smith added that the evacuees had spent only a short period in the lifeboats and were expected to be in good condition. Authorities had received no reports of injuries.

Clark said the limited information available was that the ship had struck an object and was taking on a substantial volume of water.

Forecasters told the Press Association that air temperatures in the area were about minus 5 degrees Celsius, while the sea was close to minus 1 degree Celsius. Stephen Davenport, a senior MeteoGroup forecaster, warned that immersion in water at such a temperature could cause hypothermia very quickly. He also noted that the region can experience severe storms and particularly strong, gale-force winds because there is no landmass to obstruct them.

Lt. Matt Alex of the U.S. Coast Guard’s Atlantic Area command center said the Explorer belonged to Gap Adventures, a company headquartered in Toronto, Canada.

An option to email the report to a friend accompanied the original article.

Copyright 2007 CNN. All rights reserved. The content may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. The Associated Press contributed to the report.

More than 150 people, including all 100 passengers, were evacuated into lifeboats. The captain and first officer reportedly remained aboard while nearby ships responded to the emergency.

A Norwegian rescue vessel was the first to arrive at the scene, and several other ships were dispatched to provide assistance. Although no injuries were reported, the passengers and crew faced a serious risk of hypothermia because of the subzero air and sea temperatures.
outputs.L4:
The cruise ship *Explorer* struck an iceberg near Antarctica’s South Shetland Islands and began taking on water, forcing those aboard to abandon the vessel. A distress call triggered an international rescue operation, with a Norwegian passenger ship and several other vessels in the region changing course to assist.

The *Explorer* was carrying 154 people, including passengers and crew. Passengers and most crew members were transferred into lifeboats while a small number of senior crew initially remained aboard to manage the emergency. The evacuees waited in bitterly cold conditions until the Norwegian vessel arrived and brought them to safety.

Everyone aboard was ultimately accounted for, and no injuries were reported. The successful rescue was especially significant because both the air and sea temperatures were near freezing, leaving anyone exposed—or thrown into the water—at serious risk of hypothermia. The multinational response and the presence of other ships nearby prevented the sinking from becoming a major loss-of-life disaster.
